name: Akiflow MCP
description: Akiflow connects your tasks, calendars, and meeting notes to your AI client. Read a unified schedule across every connected calendar, create and reschedule tasks, time slots, and events, and pull summaries and action items from meeting transcripts in natural language. Akiflow is the only calendar connector that aggregates multiple calendars into a single connection, so the AI sees your full schedule rather than one account at a time.

protocolMetadata.instructions:
Akiflow MCP — resource server for the Akiflow task, calendar, and productivity app. Every tool acts on behalf of the authenticated user. Datetimes are both interpreted and returned in the user's current local timezone, as naive local wall-clock with no offset (e.g. `2026-06-04T14:30:00`) — so a time read from one tool can be passed straight into another unchanged. Durations are reported in minutes.

What you can do here:
- Tasks: create, edit, complete, and trash tasks; plan a task onto a date or time, or loosely onto a whole week (plan_week) or month (plan_month); move a task back to the inbox; and list open inbox or someday tasks (list_tasks).
- Subtasks (parent/child tasks): every task reports `parent_task_id` (and `parent_task_title`), set when it is a subtask of another task. get_task on a parent additionally returns its direct children as `subtasks` — compact refs, each carrying its own `subtask_count` so you can get_task a child to reach deeper levels. To make a task a subtask, set `parent_task_id` (the parent's id) on create_task or edit_task; to move it under a different parent, set the new `parent_task_id`; to detach it into a standalone task, pass `parent_task_id: null` on edit_task. To create a parent with children, create the parent first, then create each child with its `parent_task_id` — there is no subtasks array on create. Attaching inherits the parent's project and tags for fields you leave unset. Trashing a parent detaches its direct children (they survive as standalone tasks) instead of deleting them, and completing a parent does not complete its children. A task cannot be both recurring and part of a parent/child relationship.
- Window planning: to plan a task for a week, pass plan_week as its dashed `YYYY-WW` year+week string (e.g. "2026-26" = week 26 of 2026); for a month, pass plan_month as `YYYY-MM`. Prefer these over a specific date whenever the user names a week or month without a day ("next week", "this week", "week 27", "the weekly bucke

tool.name: create_task
tool.description: Create a task for the authenticated user. Supports inbox, planned, and someday tasks, with optional priority, project, tags, deadline, location, time slot, recurrence, and links. A task can be planned loosely onto a whole week (plan_week) or month (plan_month) instead of a specific day. Datetimes are interpreted in the user's local timezone.

links.description: URLs to attach to the task as link chips — e.g. an article to read or a doc to reference. Whenever the task is about reading or pointing at a web page, put the URL here so it shows on the task. URLs you write into the title or description are detected and attached automatically, so you need not duplicate them here.

title.description: Title of the new task.

status.description: Required — always choose one explicitly; there is no default. `inbox` (unscheduled), `planned` (requires a placement: start_datetime, plan_week, or plan_month — unless recurrence is set), or `someday` (parked). Do not pass `inbox`/`someday` together with a placement — that is rejected.

deadline.description: Deadline — when the task is due — as a pure calendar date (YYYY-MM-DD). Independent of the plan date (status / start_datetime); a task in any status can have one.

duration.description: Expected duration in minutes. Optional: inbox and someday tasks have no duration unless you set one; a planned task with no duration defaults to the user's default task duration.

location.description: Where the task happens — a street address, a place name, or a meeting URL. It shows on the task, and when the task is locked to a calendar it also appears as the location of that calendar event. Single line, max 255 characters (the limit Google and Outlook accept). Pass null on edit_task to remove it.

tags_ids.description: Tag UUIDs. Unknown ids are silently filtered out.

plan_week.description: Plan the task loosely for a whole week, identified by its dashed `YYYY-WW` year+week string (e.g. "2026-26" = week 26 of 2026). Use this — not start_datetime — when the user names a week without a day ("next week", "this week", "week 27", "the weekly bucket"); don't resolve it to that week's Monday. Implies planned status. Mutually exclusive with start_datetime, plan_month, and recurrence.

plan_month.description: Plan the task loosely for a whole month, as `YYYY-MM`. Use this — not start_datetime — when the user names a month without a day ("next month", "sometime in July"). Implies planned status. Mutually exclusive with start_datetime, plan_week, and recurrence.

project_id.description: Akiflow project UUID; omit it or pass null to leave the project unspecified — a subtask then adopts its parent's project, and a task left without one may get a project predicted for it. Silently dropped if the user does not own this project.

recurrence.description: RFC 5545 RRULE string. Only honored when status=planned. Minimum frequency is daily.

section_id.description: Section (within a project) to place the task in — a section id from list_projects; null for none. The section must belong to the task's project: pass its parent as project_id, or omit project_id to adopt the section's project automatically. A section_id whose project contradicts an explicit project_id is rejected; an unknown/invalid id is silently dropped.

tool.name: get_schedule
tool.description: Read the authenticated user's schedule (tasks, events, and timeslots) over a date range. Supports overdue/completed modes, sorting, and content filters (guests, priority, duration, all-day). Durations are reported in minutes. Dates are interpreted in the user's local timezone, and all times are returned in that same timezone as naive local wall-clock (no offset) — ready to pass straight back into edit/plan tools. A task's scheduled time (date/datetime) is when to do it; its `deadline` is a separate calendar date for when it is due. `overdue` is plan-date-based (a scheduled time that has passed and is not done) and is independent of the deadline — a future-or-passed deadline alone never makes a task overdue. When `completed_mode` includes completed tasks, each completed task carries its completion time — as `done_at` (naive local wall-clock, e.g. `2026-09-09T18:23:59`) and, in the compact row, as its done badge: `[done 14:32]` when the task was completed on the row's own date, `[done Wed 9 Sep 09:05]` when it was completed on another day. Both are the same moment, distinct from the task's scheduled time, so a completed view answers "what did I finish, and when" on its own, with no get_task per row. Each event reports which calendar it is on (`calendar_name`) and, via `calendar_read_only`, whether that calendar is view-only; a view-only event's compact row is marked `[view-only]`. Such an event is one the user can only see (a subscribed or shared calendar, e.g. a spouse's): it is not the user's own commitment, so do not count it as a scheduling conflict or as something they have to attend unless the user says otherwise. tool.name: get_task
tool.description: Read a single task by its id, returning the same full detail the create/edit tools return. The id is a plain UUID, or a `parentId_originalDate` pseudoid for one instance of a recurring series. Use this to re-read a task you already hold an id for (e.g. one returned by create_task or referenced by the user) without scanning a date range with get_schedule. Trashed and cancelled tasks are reported as not found. Files attached to the task are listed under `attachments` (name, size, type, id; for a recurring occurrence, files on the whole series are included and marked so) — pass an attachment id to get_attachment to read it.

tags.description: Tags with resolved names, alongside `tags_ids`. `name` is null for an unknown id.

title.description: Always a non-empty string; "(no title)" when the task has no title.

status.description: Task placement, derived from the task: `inbox`, `someday`, `planned for <local date>` (e.g. `planned for Thu 4 Jun 14:30`), `planned for week <N> (<start> – <end>)` or `planned for <Mon YYYY>` for a window-planned task, or a terminal state such as `trashed`/`cancelled`.

done_at.description: When the task was completed, as naive local wall-clock with no offset (e.g. `2026-06-04T13:05:40`), or null when the task is not done. `done` is the boolean completion signal; this is its timestamp. Note a completed task keeps its placement `status` ("planned for …") — rely on `done`/`done_at`, not `status`, to tell whether it is finished.

datetime.description: Planned moment — when to do the task — in the user's current timezone, as naive local wall-clock with no offset (e.g. `2026-06-04T23:30:00`). Null for an all-day task (use `date`) and for unscheduled tasks. This is the plan date, not the deadline (see `deadline`). Pass it straight back to edit_task/plan_task unchanged.

tool.name: prepare_attachment_upload
tool.description:
Attach a file to a task — step one of two. This returns an `upload_url`; the file is attached once you PUT the file's exact bytes to it, and there is no further step. Only usable when you hold the file on disk AND your client can make an outbound HTTP PUT request to that URL (some hosts restrict outbound network access by default, and it may need enabling in their settings). Get the exact values first and pass them unchanged — the URL only accepts exactly `size_bytes` bytes:
  wc -c < FILE                  # size_bytes
  file --mime-type -b FILE      # mime_type
then upload:
  curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" --data-binary @FILE "<upload_url>"
The URL is valid for 30 minutes. Attaching to any task in a recurring series attaches the file to the whole series, so it appears on every occurrence — tell the user so. A task holds at most 10 files of 25 MB each, within the user's storage quota.

tool.name: get_event
tool.description: Read a single calendar event by its id, returning the same full detail get_schedule returns for an event. The id is a plain UUID for a standalone event, or a recurring occurrence id (`parentId_YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ` for timed, `parentId_YYYY-MM-DD` for all-day). Use this to re-read an event you already hold an id for without scanning a date range with get_schedule. For an all-day event, `start` and `end` are plain YYYY-MM-DD dates and `end` is INCLUSIVE — the last day the event covers, not the day after — so an absence reported as ending 2026-09-10 runs through the 10th and the person is back on the 11th; pass the value straight back to edit_event unchanged.

event_id.description: Event id. A plain UUID for a standalone event, or a recurring occurrence id (`parentId_YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ` for timed events, `parentId_YYYY-MM-DD` for all-day events).

id.description: Event id to pass back to edit_event/delete_event. For a recurring timed occurrence this is a `parentId_YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ` pseudoid; for all-day occurrences it is `parentId_YYYY-MM-DD`.

end.description: End of the event. For timed events, naive local wall-clock in the user's current timezone with no offset. For all-day events this is the INCLUSIVE last day the event covers — the last date it actually occupies, NOT the day after. A single-day event on 2026-10-04 reports end 2026-10-04, and an absence reported as end 2026-09-10 has the person back on 2026-09-11. Pass it straight back to create_event / edit_event, which read it the same way.

start.description: Start of the event. For timed events, naive local wall-clock in the user's current timezone with no offset (e.g. `2026-06-04T14:00:00`) — pass it straight back to edit_event. For all-day events, a YYYY-MM-DD date.

guests.description: Guests on the event. On a fresh create/edit preview the just-added guests appear with response_status `needsAction` and organizer false.

can_rsvp.description: Whether rsvp_event will accept a response for this event. False when the user is not a guest, the calendar is view-only, the provider has no RSVP support, or the user organizes the meeting on Outlook (which cannot express an organizer response). See `rsvp_reason`.

declined.description: Legacy synced flag, kept for compatibility: calendar-sync derives it by matching the account's email against the attendee list, ignoring the provider's `self` marker, so it can disagree with `my_response` on a shared or delegated calendar. Use `my_response` as the RSVP-authoritative field.

busy_mode.description: Whether the event marks the user busy (`opaque`) or free (`transparent`), or null when unset.

read_only.description: True when this specific occurrence cannot be edited (a busy/free import, or a Google working-location / out-of-office entry). It does not affect whether the event is the user's own commitment — use calendar_read_only for that — but it does force `can_rsvp` false.

event_type.description: Google's classification of the event, when it comes from a Google calendar: `outOfOffice`, `focusTime`, `workingLocation`, `birthday`, `fromGmail`, or `default` for an ordinary event. Null for Outlook and iCloud events, which carry no equivalent. Note that most absences people record are ordinary all-day events titled "OOO" rather than Google `outOfOffice` events, so do not treat this as a reliable way to find absences.

recurrence.description: RFC 5545 RRULE string when the event recurs, else null.

visibility.description: Event visibility (`default`, `public`, `private`), or null when unset.

my_response.description: The user's own response to this event: `accepted`, `declined`, `tentative` (shown to users as "maybe"), or `needsAction` (invited, not yet answered). `null` means the user is not a guest on the event at all — a personal calendar block, or an event on someone else's calendar. rsvp_reason.description: Why `can_rsvp` is false — the same sentence rsvp_event would refuse with. Null when the event can be responded to.

calendar_name.description: Resolved calendar name, or null when it cannot be resolved.

calendar_read_only.description: True when this event is on a calendar the user can only view (a subscribed or viewer-role shared calendar, e.g. a spouse's calendar). Do not treat such events as the user's own commitments or as scheduling conflicts unless the user explicitly says otherwise.

tool.name: rsvp_event
tool.description: Respond to a calendar invitation: accept it, decline it, or mark it as maybe (`tentative`). Use this — not edit_event — whenever the user is answering an invitation; it is the one change a guest can always make, even without permission to edit the event. Scope follows the id you pass: the exact occurrence id get_schedule returned (`parentId_YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.sssZ` for timed events, `parentId_YYYY-MM-DD` for all-day) responds for that ONE occurrence, while the plain UUID of a recurring event responds for ALL of its occurrences. Occurrences that were already answered individually keep their own response when you respond for the series; the result names them so you can respond to each separately. To respond across a date range, call get_schedule first and then this tool once per occurrence — events you are a guest on carry an `[rsvp: …]` badge. The response is queued and reported as pending until the provider applies it. Responding is refused when you are not a guest, the calendar is view-only, the provider has no RSVP support, or you organize the meeting on Outlook (which cannot express an organizer response). If asked to decline an Outlook meeting the user organizes, explain the limitation and ask whether they want to cancel it for everyone instead. Never automatically turn a decline into cancellation. An explicit organizer cancellation request uses delete_event, never rsvp_event with declined. Google organizers can still change their own RSVP without cancelling the meeting.

can_rsvp.description: Whether rsvp_event will accept a response for this event. False when the user is not a guest, the calendar is view-only, the provider has no RSVP support, or the user organizes the meeting on Outlook (which cannot express an organizer response). See `rsvp_reason`.

declined.description: Legacy synced flag, kept for compatibility: calendar-sync derives it by matching the account's email against the attendee list, ignoring the provider's `self` marker, so it can disagree with `my_response` on a shared or delegated calendar. Use `my_response` as the RSVP-authoritative field.

busy_mode.description: Whether the event marks the user busy (`opaque`) or free (`transparent`), or null when unset.

read_only.description: True when this specific occurrence cannot be edited (a busy/free import, or a Google working-location / out-of-office entry). It does not affect whether the event is the user's own commitment — use calendar_read_only for that — but it does force `can_rsvp` false.

event_type.description: Google's classification of the event, when it comes from a Google calendar: `outOfOffice`, `focusTime`, `workingLocation`, `birthday`, `fromGmail`, or `default` for an ordinary event. Null for Outlook and iCloud events, which carry no equivalent. Note that most absences people record are ordinary all-day events titled "OOO" rather than Google `outOfOffice` events, so do not treat this as a reliable way to find absences.

recurrence.description: RFC 5545 RRULE string when the event recurs, else null.

visibility.description: Event visibility (`default`, `public`, `private`), or null when unset.

my_response.description: The user's own response to this event: `accepted`, `declined`, `tentative` (shown to users as "maybe"), or `needsAction` (invited, not yet answered). `null` means the user is not a guest on the event at all — a personal calendar block, or an event on someone else's calendar. Change it with rsvp_event. Omitted on a create/edit/delete preview, which has no synced attendee list yet.

rsvp_reason.description: Why `can_rsvp` is false — the same sentence rsvp_event would refuse with. Null when the event can be responded to.

calendar_name.description: Resolved calendar name, or null when it cannot be resolved.

calendar_read_only.description: True when this event is on a calendar the user can only view (a subscribed or viewer-role shared calendar, e.g. a spouse's calendar). Do not treat such events as the user's own commitments or as scheduling conflicts unless the user explicitly says otherwise.

_published_faq.name: How do I add Akiflow MCP to Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add Akiflow MCP to Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor by connecting its remote MCP URL in each client's MCP settings. In Claude, add a custom connector.
